articles.title: Faith-Labor Organizing: Why Building Permanent Infrastructure is the Intervention This Moment Demands
articles.content: Featured image by Jared Rodriguez. Our congregations and our unions each have a measure of power. None of it is enough. The change we seek requires building power together; prioritizing building that power together in parallel with the work we are already doing alone. Our faith communities and labor unions share geographies, serve many of the same families, and claim a common commitment to human dignity. We rarely build power together. When we collaborate, the collaboration tends to be transactional: labor shows up for a rally the church organized, a pastor blesses a picket line. The event ends. Everyone goes home. No infrastructure remains. In Northern Virginia, our first Faith & Labor 2-day Training launched this April at Virginia Theological Seminary, a partnership between Virginians Organized for Interfaith Community Engagement , Virginia Theological Seminary and the Northern Virginia Labor Federation . The training brought together faith leaders, broad-based organizers and labor organizers into the same room to build shared infrastructure that outlasts any single campaign. Broad-based organizing offers labor something it cannot generate alone: deep relational practice, moral authority, and a base of power that reframes economic fights in terms that cut across partisan lines. A successful stop sign campaign at a dangerous intersection is a win. A collective bargaining contract at a single employer is a win. Neither builds the kind of power that can respond when a state agency is dismantled or when a national crisis demands coordinated action across regions. We need shared infrastructure: durable, adaptable, that can address systemic challenges affecting workers and their families, not just the local fights we can win alone. History is unambiguous: when worker rights and the moral arc of humanity advance most, faith communities and labor are in the trenches together. The abolitionist movement; the eight-hour workday; the sanitation worker strike in Memphis, where Martin Luther King Jr. died supporting a union strike. Civil rights and labor rights were never separate fights–they were the same fight, waged by people who understood that dignity is indivisible. When these movements separated, both weakened. Both institutions are losing members. Neither is losing infrastructure. Union halls still exist in every major metro area. Churches, mosques, and synagogues still anchor neighborhoods. When autocracy rises, it targets unions and prophetic religion, because organized workers and organized faith are the two forces that can mobilize people across race, geography, and class. Preventing a slide into autocracy requires these two traditions to be intentional and intentionality requires material investment in organizing money and people. It is also to recognize that the light at the end of the tunnel only becomes possible when labor and faith communities are joined tightly in the shared struggle for dignity. That history drove the partnership. But the immediate spark was simpler: we are organizing the same people separately, often for related fights, without knowing it. Three years ago, I began one-on-ones with labor leaders across Northern Virginia. The conversations revealed mutual frustration and mutual suspicion. Some union organizers saw faith communities as naïve, focused on charity rather than power. Some clergy saw labor as transactional, insufficiently concerned with the whole person and only looking to “rent a clergy” for rallies or strikes. Both sides had been burned by partnerships that felt extractive: show up for our event, lend us your credibility, then disappear. The breakthrough came when we stopped talking about collaboration and started practicing it. We plan to run joint listening sessions in congregations with a focus on speaking with private sector workers. We are in active practice of inviting labor organizers to observe our leadership development and vice versa–the traditions, while different, are not incompatible; they are complementary. A critical insight: each side must not feel the other is paternalistic or lecturing on how the other should organize. Labor has a century of hard-won wisdom about building power against adversaries with resources to crush you. Faith communities have centuries of practice holding people together through suffering, building the relational density that sustains movements across generations. We each have something to teach. We each have something to learn. The partnership only works if both sides believe that. Sixty million American workers say they would join a union if they could. Public approval of unions sits at 70 percent, near a sixty-year high. Meanwhile, union density continues to fall. The desire is there but the infrastructure to convert that desire into organized power is not. Church membership has fallen below 50 percent for the first time in Gallup’s history. Weekly attendance sits around 20 percent. Both institutions are losing members. Neither is losing infrastructure. Union halls still exist in every major metro area. Churches, mosques, and synagogues still anchor neighborhoods. What has eroded is the relational tissue between us, our leaders, and the communities we serve. Broad-based organizing offers labor something it cannot generate alone: deep relational practice, moral authority, and a base of power that reframes economic fights in terms that cut across partisan lines. Labor offers a rich history of disruptive power, grit, experience in the trenches, and organized workers with economic leverage that can translate moral witness into material wins. The planning process surfaced differences as expected. Language was the first negotiation. Labor organizers use “campaign” to mean a sustained, escalating fight with a clear target and timeline. Broad-based organizers use the word “campaign” more loosely than our labor counterparts do. For us, a campaign is the whole life cycle of an issue, not just the final push. That sounds like a small distinction until you try to build a strategy on top of it. We had to agree on the meaning of the words before we could agree on what to do. So we studied a fight that had already lived through that question, a worker led campaign over a public transit system in the City of Alexandria, Virginia, that showed us what solidarity between faith and labor actually looks like in practice. In 2018, drivers at DASH, the City of Alexandria’s public bus system, voted 97 to 13 to join Amalgamated Transit Union Local 689. DASH (unofficially known as Driving Alexandria Safely Home) is run as a nonprofit and staffs its workforce through a private company. The drivers earned less than nearby counterparts, and it took the drivers, prior to this campaign, over 20 years just to reach a top wage of $29 an hour. The fight had become a learning touchstone for the leaders gathered in April, trying to figure out how faith and labor can build together, because it served as an example of what it looks like to find solidarity between two sets of priorities. Pace is a point of divergence between broad-based organizing and labor organizing. Union campaigns run on tight deadlines. A contract expires, an election gets scheduled, management pushes back, and the deadline is non-negotiable. Broad-based organizing moves more consistently at the pace of trust, which can feel painfully slow to a colleague staring down a calendar but both have instances in which organizing conditions are interchangeable. Broad-based can have tight deadlines and labor can and does, at times, move at the pace of trust. The DASH fight shows the solidarity between the two, and it shows an example of a way forward. ATU had a hard date for a unionization election. But the foundation underneath that sprint was relational, and it was built one driver at a time. Organizers met drivers at the Subway down the street from the garage. They rode Metro dressed as passengers to talk with drivers off the clock. They learned that junior drivers had to be approached before senior drivers, who carried more resistance, and that reaching the Ethiopian drivers in the workforce meant bringing in someone those drivers already knew. When public pressure finally arrived, it landed on a base that had been built quietly for months. The sprint won the vote, 97 to 13. The trust made the sprint possible. We are still figuring out how to honor both rhythms, but DASH suggests we don’t have to choose. The surprises have been generative. Labor organizers were startled by how directly faith leaders talk about self-interest; not as selfishness but as the engine of sustainable commitment. Faith leaders were startled by how precisely labor organizers track power: who has it, who wants it, what they will do to keep it. The traditions are more compatible than either side assumed. VOICE is a founding affiliate of the Just Power Alliance, launched in 2024. The Alliance’s nine founding affiliates represent roughly 330 institutions and organize over half a million people across the East Coast, Mid-Atlantic, and Great Lakes. After Virginia, the model could scale across the network: DC, Maryland, Boston, Milwaukee, Cleveland, Connecticut. Each geographic location is anchored in local faith-labor partnerships. The vision is not a new national organization. It is national infrastructure; organizers and leaders in different cities, fluent in the same skills and in more than one organizing tradition, who can support one another’s campaigns and develop leaders who move between the sanctuary and the union hall. Organized money benefits from the division between faith and labor. When we fight housing battles without labor’s economic leverage, we lose. When we fight contract battles without faith communities’ moral authority, we fight alone. The structural separation between our movements is not inevitable. It is a condition we can organize against. If you are an organizer, a pastor, a rabbi, an imam, a union leader, or a lay leader, the question is whether you will prioritize building power with people outside your institution along with the work you are already doing inside it. If you believe the change you seek requires building the power to achieve it, your answer should be yes.

articles.title: Trump’s Greenland Deal Puts His Annexation Plans on Ice
articles.author: Huw Paige
articles.content: Donald Trump recently concluded an agreement with the governments of Greenland and Denmark over the status of the Arctic island. Trump presented it as a big victory for his efforts, claiming that it granted the United States “permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many US concerns.” The substance of the agreement told a different story. After doing lasting damage to the relationship between the United States and Europe, the Trump administration got more or less the same deal it could have obtained by asking politely. Trump’s repeatedly stated plan to acquire Greenland has been put on the back burner. End of the Saga? “Greenland belongs to the Greenlanders — it cannot be taken from us,” Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens Frederik Nielsen proclaimed in a Facebook post that showed him grinning contentedly. A saga that has brought hitherto unprecedented attention to his country seemed to be coming to an end. The deal , signed by the leaders of Greenland, Denmark, and the United States at the United Nations General Assembly in New York, permits the US to open two bases in Greenland, Mestersvig in the east and Narsarsuaq in the south. Mestersvig is a base for the Sirius Patrol, a dogsled unit of the Danish military operating in the remote Northeast Greenland National Park. Narsarsuaq is an airfield that was constructed during the World War II as a US airbase and that closed as an international airport earlier this year. A recent investigation by the Danish newspaper Politiken found that when the Americans left most of their Greenlandic bases after finding Cold War replacements for them, they abandoned “several thousand tons of hazardous or contaminated waste.” At Narsarsuaq, this waste material included oil drums and asbestos sheets scattered around the old base. The Trump administration has presented this outcome as a vindication of its strategy. But the United States has long been able to construct new facilities in Greenland if it has the consent of the other parties. The 1951 Defense of Greenland Agreement , reached after the US had taken responsibility for Greenland’s security during Denmark’s wartime occupation, established this principle. The negotiations that have proceeded in earnest since the start of 2026 could have happened without any US threats to take control of the island. “Sensitive Sectors” However, the new agreement does contain several changes in other areas. Whereas the 1951 agreement was valid for as long as NATO existed, the new version, officially intending to “amend and supplement” the old one, stresses its permanence and includes provisions for a future independent Greenland. At the same time, it requires that an independent Greenland “agree to remain in NATO, including by applying to become a member if necessary.” This suggests that some commentary inspired by the absence of any reference to NATO in Trump’s post was slightly overblown. In other respects, the deal formalizes an unwritten understanding that investment in “sensitive sectors or activities” by non-NATO states is unwelcome. This understanding was already clear during the first Trump administration, when Denmark provided funding for Greenlandic airport upgrades to avoid a hostile US reaction over potential Chinese investment in the project. Back in 2016, Denmark rejected a Chinese bid to take over the Kangilinnguit naval base due to “security concerns.” China’s much-vaunted Arctic ambitions have been constrained in recent years. While the exact meaning of the term “sensitive” is open to debate, the US seems to have obtained an effective veto over any future Russian or Chinese presence in Greenland. Questions also remain elsewhere: the agreement does not address the question of resource extraction in Greenland (apart from a clause that prohibits “control” or “strong influence” by non-NATO states and investors, unless the parties agree that their activities “would not constitute a threat to national security or public order”). Trump’s threats prompted the formation of a unity government after the last election, with four of the five parties in the Greenlandic parliament taking part before one withdrew earlier this year. This means that policy differences between its constituent parties over this question have been left unresolved. Demokraatit, the party of Greenland’s prime minister, Jens Frederik Nielsen, is in favor of extraction, while Inuit Ataqatigiit, the party of his foreign minister, Múte Egede, takes a different stance. It won the 2021 Greenlandic election on a platform of opposition to a uranium and rare earth mining project in the country’s south. Disputes between the Greenlandic government and a US oil firm with links to Trump have sporadically flared up over the question of which licenses it needs and whether the licenses it already has access to are valid. If these disputes drag on into next summer, and Trump-friendly figures within Greenland Energy get the president’s ear, things could erupt again. An agreement on security does not preclude a later dispute on other issues, especially where there is money to be made. White Gold Rush Although some elements of the deal could prove consequential, its most significant part may well be the opening preamble. For the first time in the relationship between Greenland and the United States, this is an agreement negotiated from the outset by a Greenlandic government. In January 2026, two Inuit scholars released a briefing paper on the ongoing impact of colonization on Greenland. Vivi Vold and Kunuk (Sandra) Inutiq highlighted Washington’s “imperialist and colonialist” rhetoric but stressed that Denmark could not “demand silence” on other topics in the name of unity against the United States. Two of the cases that they mentioned bear repeating here. First, disgraceful episodes such as the implantation of IUDs into thousands of Inuit women and girls between the 1960s and the 1980s, many of whom did not give their consent, remain unresolved. Rival reports were released in August this year, after a group of four experts could not agree on a verdict. The report released by the Greenlandic government suggested that the term “genocide,” which Múte Egede had used during his time as prime minister, could not be ruled out. The other report, produced by two of the experts who split from the government-backed group, reached a less strident conclusion. Neither report had a Greenlandic Inuit coauthor. Second, mining of the mineral cryolite, which is important for the production of aluminium, generated vast amounts of wealth for Denmark in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. As it happens, the naval base China unsuccessfully sought to purchase in 2016 was originally constructed by the US Navy to protect the very same cryolite mine. In Greenland, American influence is never far away. There was a fierce controversy in Denmark after the public service broadcaster DR released a documentary called Greenland’s White Gold in the buildup to the 2025 Greenlandic election. The documentary attempted to calculate the scale of this windfall and suggested that it may have amounted to 400 billion kroner in today’s money. By making this calculation, the program makers sought to push back against a persistent Danish idea that Denmark’s contribution to the Greenlandic government budget is akin to a generous gift. An economist who had appeared in the documentary questioned one of its core calculations, and the Danish culture minister strongly criticized it. After initially standing by the program, DR pulled it from its streaming service, and a senior editor resigned. The fact that an issue like this could flare up at the height of the “Greenland crisis” reveals the deep feelings that persist within what many still view as a colonial relationship. US posturing has disrupted Denmark’s gradual acknowledgment of its history with Greenland, allowing the former colonizer to portray itself as a protective elder sibling. No Good Colonizers The standoff has also diverted attention from other domestic issues. In May 2025, local hotel owner Mike Nicolaisen organized a protest against the lack of investment in Tasiilaq, the largest settlement on Greenland’s east coast. Six hundred people — one-third of the town’s population and nearly a sixth of the entire region’s inhabitants — showed up. Nicolaisen and his wife, Anette, subsequently announced the formation of a new “Party for an Independent East Greenland.” In an interview with KNR, Greenland’s national broadcaster, he described the protest as a “cry for help” and said that the aspirant party was necessary to bring attention to his region: “The only time we’re remembered is when it’s about suicide, misery, and alcohol.” Decades of underinvestment in the regions and a lack of employment opportunities has drawn people to move either to the capital, Nuuk, or to Copenhagen. Population growth in Nuuk has kept house prices extremely high, combined with slow construction rates and the difficulty of finding empty land on the rocky peninsula upon which the city is situated. There is also a significant problem of homelessness. The Greenlandic government cannot trust that this new deal will permanently satisfy the United States. But skilful negotiation by the Danish and Greenlandic governments has avoided a doomsday scenario. Trump is now claiming a win at little cost to his negotiating partners, and arguments over resource extraction have been deferred. Now that the specter of Greenland’s potential seizure by force has been put to bed for the time being, there is more space for reckoning with the ongoing legacies of colonization, which can help prevent the formation of new relationships based on similar premises. Trump may have brought Denmark and Greenland closer together, but there is still no such thing as a better colonizer.

articles.title: Buffalo DSA Leaders Meet With Rep. AOC
articles.author: Buffalo DSA
articles.content: On Thursday, members of our Steering Committee and endorsed candidate Adam Bojak met privately with Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. We were proud to share how we are building a durable, sustainable socialist project here, as well as share our hope to see Rep. AOC coordinate more strongly with the growing socialist bloc forming at every level of elected office. Afterward, a range of our chapter organizers joined Team AOC for their Project Reactivation event. Regardless of what her political career holds, one thing is clear: Rep. AOC and her team would not have visited Buffalo, or prioritized a private sit-down with Buffalo DSA leaders, without the diligent work of our members. The foundation we’ve laid in healthcare organizing, labor solidarity, tenant suport, and electoral politics have put Buffalo DSA on the map. The working class is hungry for political change, and our chapter is ready to lead the charge. We look forward to leading discussions on this meeting, how our chapter might relate to a future AOC candidacy, and more at our Oct. 17 General Body Meeting. We will also hold our first of many discussions on the 2028 Presidential Election, and DSA’s role within that. Join DSA to shape our strategy in and out of electoral politics, to build real working class power.

articles.title: We Have to Figure Out How to Design a Warming Planet
articles.author: Marianela D’Aprile
articles.content: Before we get into the nitty-gritty, we should start with the problem in its purest form: The world as we know it cannot go on. Something’s got to give. Ideally, that would be capitalism, but we don’t have enough time to pull that off before the planet catches fire. The planet is already catching fire. What to do, then? Everything — supply chains, information systems, labor practices, policy decisions, economic structures­ — is so inextricably linked that it feels impossible to know where to start chipping away. Recently a friend asked, hypothetically, why it would be worthwhile to make an ethical decision in one’s own personal life if the larger entities that structure that life certainly aren’t making ethical decisions. Isn’t their impact much larger than our own? It’s hard to argue with that.In the design world, the responses to what I’ve come to think of as “scalar overwhelm” (often accompanied by a sense of nihilism) have ranged from cynical surrender — if you can’t beat them, join them: design for developers, make some money, and call it a day — to fantastical idealism: draw up “solutions” to the crises we face that will be hard to build and even harder to finance. Architects and designers are often left out of the funding and policy decision-making processes that structure and condition their work, meaning that the work they do is often reactive rather than proactive. More often than not, an architect’s job is to design to minimize up-front costs and maximize return on investment for developers.When that’s your everyday task, it’s difficult to imagine how you might participate in ameliorating global warming, a crisis to which your job directly contributes — buildings and their construction account for about 40 percent of all greenhouse gases globally — but cannot directly solve. It’s not exactly up to you how the concrete panels you specified in your design plan are manufactured, what fuel the truck that transports wood to the job site uses, or whether the grid your building connects to runs on fossil fuels.Fortunately, Damian White and Nicholas Pevzner have written a book that will help almost anyone — primarily but not solely architects and designers — put some detail on the source of their scalar overwhelm and thereby make it more approachable. Designing the Just Transition is not a blueprint; it is a topographical map of the way designers and design thinkers have tried to address our warming planet and the factors that might facilitate (or make difficult) the collective creation of a new world.Ambitious! And why shouldn’t it be? In Designing’s lengthy introduction, White and Pevzner lay out the stakes: the world is not only warming, it is unstable and unlikely to stabilize any time soon. And yet it is still imperative that we do something to improve life upon it.Within this fractious context, White and Pevzner attempt to “consider what opening might exist for a design- and labor-friendly politics of transition that can revitalize the public imagination and the public realm.” For them, a “just transition” is not merely a set of policies: it is a “demand for a future that ties the social question and the ecology question together.” In order to find an opening for it, White and Pevzner look both backward and forward.The first three chapters situate us in design and labor histories, tracing, respectively, the often contentious relationship between the labor and environmental movements; the history of environmental, ecological, and “nature-inspired” design; and the ways the architecture and planning industries have interacted (or not) with the concept of green design. To those versed in labor or design histories, much of the content of these chapters will be familiar. White and Pevzner’s contribution in this first half of the book is to bring all of these histories together under a singular frame. To those not so versed in these topics, Designing’s first three chapters will serve as a crash course, helpfully focused by the book’s political orientation and aims.In its fourth chapter, Designing begins to look toward the future. The question mark that punctuates its title, “Labor-Centered and Worker-Centered Design for Just Transitions?”, implies doubt: Is this quest even possible? White and Pevzner suggest that it might be, first by surfacing histories of design initiatives that brought together environmental and labor concerns, and then by visiting contemporary currents of design doing the same.This dual endeavor marks the book’s pivot point. From here on, it’s all about the hereafter. Chapters five, six, and seven consider, respectively, the role of noncredentialed designers in cocreating the future, exploring the contributions and limitations of the field of critical design studies; the role of the Green New Deal in advancing conversations about design, labor, and decarbonization; and the possibilities modeled, proposed, and speculated upon in “political theory, [climate fiction], speculative design futuring, and contemporary design practice.”The mere act of considering these questions is one of optimism, but White and Pevzner aren’t prescriptive. They are at their best when laying out the stakes and illuminating some of the stones that might pave a path forward, as in this passage:The core position here . . . is that life on a hotter, more turbulent, and more dynamic planet will require design interventions that will have to be iterative and inventive, taking place again and again and again in climate-challenged worlds. The general proposition that design would do well to orientate itself toward a dynamic future “coming at us” has much greater alignment with more recent developments in non-equilibrium ecology, climate science, and complexity theory than a great deal of equilibrium orientated ecological design of the past.This orientation toward the world’s inherent instability runs through Designing and is perhaps the book’s guiding principle: that it is the task of those demanding a just transition to imagine adaptation as an ongoing process that necessarily accommodates perpetual change. In that process, design can neither be dismissed as inert nor centered as the only way toward a solution; labor must be considered and accounted for; and sustainability must be a goal but not the goal, rather part of a constellation of characteristics of a fairer society that also include “meaningful work, labor, wellbeing, economic security, and shared prosperity.”Despite their optimism, or maybe because of it, White and Pevzner end Designing by addressing the disenchanted quality of our current moment: the pervasive scalar nihilism. They write:The just transition irreducibly raises questions about the extent to which we can plan, design, redesign, imagine, and materialize worlds that are very different to business as usual or the extent to which the forces of the status quo will lock us into fossil capitalism and life on a much warmer, more turbulent planet.In the face of these questions, it would be easy to shrug, cowed by their magnitude into inaction. The merit of White and Pevzner’s book is in expanding upon, elucidating, and contextualizing these questions, engaging with the many thinkers, academics, theorists, and writers that have asked or anticipated them. If Designing the Just Transition is a topographical map, then after reading it, we might not know when the next earthquake is coming, but we will know where the fault lines are — and where we might find the footholds necessary to climb a seemingly unscalable mountain.

articles.title: Mark Carney Is Taking Aim at Canada’s Labor Movement
articles.author: Adam D. K. King
articles.content: On September 21, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government introduced legislation that could amount to one of the most significant rollbacks of workers’ rights in Canada since the creation of the postwar industrial relations system. Tucked inside the sprawling 232-page Bill C-39 are amendments to the Canada Labour Code that would give the federal labor minister explicit authority to terminate lawful strikes and impose binding dispute resolution when the minister decides a work stoppage threatens the “national interest.” The legislation would also create a new “special mediator,” adding an additional state-directed phase to collective bargaining. Before workers can strike, the mediator would produce a report on bargaining disputes, which the minister would make public if the parties fail to reach an agreement. The new process would create a new perquisite for eventual government intervention under the controversial Section 107 of the Labour Code. The government describes these provisions as “guardrails” constraining ministerial power. But they are anything but. The legislation instead doubles down on what has become a pattern of strikebreaking from the Liberals. These proposed changes to labor law fit within Carney’s broader corporate remodeling of Canada. In response to Donald Trump’s trade war, the Liberals are attempting to attract domestic and international capital through lower investment taxes, accelerated project approvals, privatization, and a political commitment to ensuring that infrastructure gets built quickly. Workers’ capacity to disrupt the movement of goods and capital poses an obvious complication for such a project. Bill C-39 is the government’s answer. From Section 107 to the “National Interest” The attack on the right to strike did not begin with Bill C-39. Over the past two years, Liberal labor ministers have repeatedly used Section 107 of the Canada Labour Code to terminate strikes or lockouts and send disputes to the Canada Industrial Relations Board, often resulting in binding arbitration. The provision has been deployed in disputes involving railworkers at Canadian National Railway Company and Canadian Pacific Kansas City, West Coast and Quebec port workers , Canada Post employees, WestJet mechanics , and Air Canada flight attendants . The result has been a creeping normalization of extraordinary government intervention into union negotiations. Section 107 itself says little more than that the minister may take measures deemed necessary to “maintain or secure industrial peace.” Until recently, the provision was not generally understood as a standing power allowing a minister to effectively accomplish by executive order what governments historically required back-to-work legislation to achieve. Unions have responded with constitutional challenges. Teamsters Canada challenged the government’s intervention in the 2024 railway dispute; the Canadian Union of Postal Workers challenged the intervention that suspended its 2024 strike; and the Canadian Union of Public Employees (CUPE) has contested Ottawa’s use of Section 107 against Air Canada flight attendants in 2025. Instead of retreating from this experiment, the government launched a truncated review of the Labour Code seemingly meant to supercharge its recent interventionism. The process quickly raised alarms among unions. The first consultation ran from April 17 to May 25 of this year and canvassed dozens of potentially consequential changes to federal labor law. A second consultation , focused partly on Section 107, ran from July 3 until August 2. Unifor complained that the exercise gave unions only limited time to respond to a broad range of questions concerning fundamental changes to collective bargaining law. In its second submission , the union again warned that the abbreviated process was particularly troubling when Charter-protected bargaining and strike rights were at stake. Bill C-39 shows why those concerns were justified. The bill creates a special mediation process for certain difficult bargaining relationships. The mediator would attempt to secure an agreement before a strike or lockout begins. Failing that, they would issue a report outlining the issues, the parties’ positions, and recommendations. That report would become public, ostensibly to put pressure on unions to concede. But the mediator has another significance. Everyone at the bargaining table will know that the next step is binding arbitration. The rewritten Section 107 would expressly permit the minister, once a strike or lockout begins, to direct the Canada Industrial Relations Board to restore operations, extend a collective agreement, or impose binding arbitration if the minister believes the dispute “adversely affects or may adversely affect the national interest.” “National interest” is an enormously elastic concept. The legislation identifies economic effects and serious social disruption as considerations, alongside freedom of association, but ultimately leaves the decision solely with the minister. The danger this poses extends well beyond strikes that get terminated. Employers bargain differently when they believe the state will eventually rescue them from the economic consequences of job action. The threat of intervention therefore tips the bargaining balance in favor of employers before workers even erect a picket line. Teamsters Canada says this is precisely what happened during the 2024 railway dispute. “The government has created an environment that will no longer provide employers with the incentive to bargain in good faith,” Teamsters Canada President François Laporte said after Bill C-39 was introduced. Making Canada Safe for Investment Bill C-39 makes considerably more sense when viewed alongside Carney’s wider economic program. The Trump administration’s escalating trade war has thrown Canada’s economic model into crisis. For decades, Canadian governments pursued ever-deeper integration with the United States. Carney’s response to the breakdown of that relationship has been to promise that Canada can reinvent itself as a destination for global investment while rapidly expanding energy, mining, transportation, defense, and artificial intelligence infrastructure. Central to that project is the government’s Major Projects Office , established in 2025 to accelerate what Ottawa calls “nation-building” projects. Bill C-39 extends this agenda by seeking a “one project, one review, one year” standard for federal approvals. The government argues that faster decisions can coexist with environmental protections and indigenous rights. Critics, however, have questioned whether compressing approval processes can preserve meaningful democratic participation. Environmental reviews, indigenous consultations, regulatory hearings, and collective bargaining all take time. Strikes can halt ports, railways, airlines, and other infrastructure through which commodities and capital circulate. For a government promising investors “speed, certainty, and predictability,” these democratic and collective processes are obstacles. Carney made the government’s priorities remarkably explicit at this month’s Canada Investment Summit in Toronto. The event brought together investors from nearly thirty countries managing more than $100 trillion in assets. Ottawa says the summit produced commitments approaching $500 billion and is part of a strategy to catalyze $1 trillion in investment over five years. Carney told investors that his government was pursuing some of Canada’s most significant regulatory reforms in generations and promised that “when Canada says it wants something built, Canada will get it built.” He also announced a major expansion of business investment deductions that the government says will reduce Canada’s marginal effective tax rate on new investment from roughly 13 percent to 6.4 percent. And then there is privatization. At the same summit, Carney announced plans to solicit private investment through long-term concessions to operate Canada’s four largest airports — Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal, and Calgary. Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives Senior Economist David Macdonald has warned that airport privatization converts public, nonprofit infrastructure into a vehicle for extracting returns. Because airports possess considerable monopoly power, he argues, private operators can generate profits through higher charges, reduced service quality, contracting out, layoffs, and downward pressure on wages. Seen in this context, Bill C-39 is not an isolated labor law reform. It belongs to a larger political-economic project aimed at reorganizing Canada around corporate priorities. The government is offering investors lower taxes, fewer regulations, new infrastructure opportunities, and access to formerly nonprofit public assets. It is simultaneously proposing greater state power over workers capable of disrupting the transportation networks on which that investment strategy depends. Canadian business organizations have long complained about strikes at ports, railways and airlines. Bill C-39 translates that concern with “certainty” into regressive labor law reform. The state now reserves the authority to decide when workers’ economic power has become inconsistent with the “national interest.” Is Canadian Labor Up for the Fight? Unions have reacted angrily. The Canadian Labour Congress , Unifor , Teamsters Canada , and provincial labor federations have all condemned the proposed restrictions. The Canadian Union of Public Employees has gone furthest. On September 23, its national executive board unanimously resolved that the union would defy Bill C-39's strike restrictions if Parliament passes the legislation unamended. That threat could prove consequential. Air Canada flight attendants represented by CUPE refused to immediately return to work after the government used Section 107 against their strike in August 2025, continuing their walkout even after the labor board declared it unlawful. Whether the broader labor movement is willing to commit to bold action remains to be seen. The stakes are high. The postwar system of industrial legality is being fundamentally challenged by employers and governments alike. Labor rights that governments can suspend whenever they become economically disruptive risk becoming no rights at all. Bill C-39 therefore poses a strategic challenge for organized labor. Statements, lobbying, and constitutional litigation can all shape what happens next. But the history of union struggles in Canada and beyond shows that the effectiveness of labor rights depends heavily on workers’ capacity to exercise collective power. The Carney government is attempting to build a political economy organized around reassuring investors that Canada will be fast, predictable, and profitable. Whether workers’ right to withdraw their labor remains an effective counterweight will depend substantially on how unions respond.

articles.title: The Dilemmas of Socialist Governance of a Capitalist State
articles.author: Max Elbaum
articles.content: Since the 2016 combination of Donald Trump’s election and Bernie Sanders’s breakthrough campaign, efforts to synergize grassroots organizing with electoral engagement have become a priority for both long-standing and new radical formations. The dominant strategy is for socialists and progressives to run as Democrats aiming to both block MAGA’s drive toward US-style fascism and to win a measure of Left “ governing power .” In the last year, such efforts have yielded impressive results. Zohran Mamdani, a democratic socialist, is mayor of the nation’s largest city. Abdul El-Sayed, an outspoken advocate for Medicare for All and Palestinian rights, won the Democratic nomination for US senator in Michigan. More than a dozen sitting congressmembers are champions of Justice Democrats , the Working Families Party (WFP), or the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), and their number is likely to grow following the midterms. A serious conversation is underway about the broad Left rallying behind a movement-identified candidate for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination. That person ( Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is the most-talked about choice) would run not just to promote radical ideas or influence the eventual nominee but to win. It’s a promising start , and prospects are good for its momentum to continue . But it will take orders of magnitude more wins for this radical insurgency to match the strength of either MAGA or the long-standing Democratic Party leadership, much less exceed it. Portions of the Left think this is a mistaken path. Some critics think electoral engagement is worthless. Others believe that fighting on Democratic Party terrain for any goal other than breaking off to form a workers’ party as soon as possible inevitably leads to compromises that undermine the working-class movement. But these critics are on the defensive. Insurgent campaigns in Democratic primaries have clearly contributed to the spread of anti-capitalist ideas and the growth of radical and socialist organizations. Left-wing electeds — Mamdani in particular — have produced gains for (and mitigated harms against) workers and the popular majority while promoting immigrant rights, anti-racism, and opposition to US support for Israel’s Gaza genocide. In contrast, electoral abstentionism and third-party-ism have failed historically and currently to gain mass traction or provide a practical way of getting MAGA out of power. The critics therefore lack an attractive alternative to offer. Still, there is unease about pursuing a “governing power” strategy among some whose practical work meshes with it. For activists who have decided that only replacing capitalism with socialism can bring about a world of peace and justice, the recent hard-won electoral wins are gratifying but leave unanswered questions. For good reason, there is doubt that electoral victories, even when backed by powerful grassroots-based organizations, will get us to socialism. Isn’t the very structure of the capitalist state a barrier against working-class power? Don’t we need to dismantle, rather than govern, the US state? How does what we are doing today give us a North Star we can follow to a socialist horizon? There are no ready-made answers to these questions. For more than a century, dedicated revolutionaries have grappled theoretically and practically with how to get to socialism in a capitalist country with a developed economy and electoral system. No one has succeeded. Anyone who says “this is the way” is overpromising. Still, much has been learned about which approaches hold the most potential. There is overwhelming evidence that the fight for governing power within capitalism is a stage of struggle that cannot be skipped. Rather, it is necessary to develop a working-class-led movement broad enough, rooted enough, savvy enough, and positioned well enough to bring about a “ revolutionary rupture ” that dismantles the capitalist state if and when conditions to do so (a “ revolutionary situation ”) arise. I make a case here for that perspective and point toward some resources that help us both navigate this stage and gain a clearer sense of what we will confront in the next one. An Underlying Contradiction The first step in making this argument is squarely facing the complicated dilemma that faces those of us pursuing a “governing power” strategy, even if we are only beginning to experience its concrete manifestations. That dilemma is aptly characterized in a recent Jacobin article by Peter Frase, “Zohran Mamdani and the Contradiction of Democratic Socialism.” Frase points out that there is a contradiction “between Mamdani as a product of DSA, an organization at least nominally aiming to overturn the capitalist mode of production, and Mamdani as a politician attempting to operate the machinery of the capitalist state apparatus.” The piece describes different left approaches to navigating the Mamdani-in-office terrain. These vary from activists “who see the task of DSA as defending Mamdani’s policy agenda and building the base of popular support for it . . . [to] those more concerned with calling out compromises or betrayals that separate the new mayor’s actions in power from the principles of a democratic socialist organization.” The debate between these poles persists because, as Frase points out, it is rooted in a contradiction that must be understood in “a Marxist sense: an antagonism that cannot be resolved without overcoming the larger system that gives rise to it, such as that between capital and labor.” Given the messiness of that debate and, more fundamentally, the inherent problem of uncomfortable compromises, alliances, and governing policy dilemmas it reflects, there is an understandable desire to bypass the problem by refraining from participation within any component part of the capitalist state. But giving in to that temptation in a country with even a relatively weak electoral system (much less a rooted one like the United States) is self-marginalizing. The modern state is an instrument of class rule, but it is simultaneously a terrain of class struggle . Messy as it is, the Left must find a way to navigate the contradictions built into fighting for and winning a measure of governing power — including at the federal level, where the contradiction is especially sharp, since the US state remains an anchor of an imperialist system even in its period of decline. With the State, Against the State, Beyond the State A core component of this argument is that the fight for and deployment of governing power includes but is broader than contesting elections and winning office. It is a full-spectrum struggle that must include battle on the economic, cultural, institution-building, and narrative (ideological) fronts to build sufficient strength of the popular classes outside the state to drive the process. The components of a comprehensive governing power strategy can be captured in a phrase taken from the South African left: “ With the state, against the state, beyond the state ”: With the state : Contest elections. Become a force in the legislative, executive, and judicial branches of government at the local, state, and federal levels. Pursue a “ co-governance ” approach to create an ongoing and generative dynamic between elected officials and the social base that put them in office. By wielding accumulated strength inside and outside the state, deliver material gains, expand democratic space, minimize harm, and gain a deep understanding of what policies work in a complex society with a tremendously diverse working class. Against the state : Continue to make demands on the state and fight for them, which sometimes will mean pushing officials we support and sometimes opposing them. Beyond the state : This component has a double meaning. First, it means that building the organized, institutional strength of workers and all the oppressed outside the state (trade unions, community organizations, a media apparatus, narrative and cultural power, etc.) is indispensable. Second, it means that the most conscious portion of the popular insurgency understands that holding governing power in a capitalist state creates a contradictory and unstable situation. At some point, it will be resolved either by the progressives and socialists being driven back or by a radical rupture that dismantles the existing state structure and puts a new structure in place. A corollary to both of these meanings is that every possible step is taken to weaken the state structures that are most tied to maintaining capitalism, whatever amount of governing power the Left holds at a given time. Purely Outside Will Not Work The above is a bare-bones outline that needs a great deal of fleshing out as the Left gains experience in its practical application. At the moment, fighting for left governing power in ways that facilitate building a front broad and strong enough to oust MAGA is a prime concern. If we succeed in pushing US fascism back, the challenges of fighting for and deploying governing power in a period more favorable for left advance will come to the fore. We need to expect setbacks. But there are several reasons to pursue this course even at moments when we are confronted with how difficult it is. The first is that attempting to overturn a developed capitalist state solely by acting outside the state is extremely unlikely to work. That course has been tried by substantial portions of the Left in the US and elsewhere over the last one hundred years and never came anywhere near success. Such efforts have never gained as much strength as projects that have fought for influence inside as well as outside the capitalist state. There is a structural reason for this: the effect that substantial electoral systems have on the dynamics of mass politics. These systems offer a route to changing the conditions of life and expanding the democratic rights of workers and the oppressed. That is why movements for workers and oppressed peoples have fought for universal suffrage and fair elections since Karl Marx’s time. In the United States, the fight for black voting rights in the arc from abolitionism to Reconstruction and then, in the 1950s–’60s, the Second Reconstruction, has been among the most bitter, violent, and consequential in the nation’s history. Most socialists, while participating in these fights, have concluded from their theoretical reflection and historical analysis that socialism will not be achieved via elections. But the mass of the working class and its allies learn that lesson through their own experience ; that is, through traveling the electoral route and pushing it to its limits. Left propaganda plays an important role in driving home the point, but that role is secondary to the direct experience of millions in struggle. This stage of mass engagement may be long or short, and it is possible that a moment of decisive confrontation with capital may come before the popular bloc attains all the governing power within capitalism that it aims for. But the point is, this stage of struggle cannot be skipped. Social Welfare Programs via the State An additional factor that pulls mass struggles into the quest for governing power is the evolution of the capitalist state since the debates over works such as Vladimir Lenin’s The State and Revolution shaped the modern socialist movement. At that time, the operational components of capitalist states overwhelmingly if not exclusively consisted of the military, the police, and a bureaucracy for tax collection. The modern state has expanded with many additional functions, including large-scale oversight and delivery of “welfare state” programs. Such programs are taken on by the state because it is pressed to do so by the struggles of workers and their allies. These struggles are ongoing; working-class movements almost universally demand the protection and expansion of such programs and introduction of new ones. This is a way for the mass of workers and the poor to win benefits that, even if they could be gained from specific employers, would only accrue to a limited number. For example, today one of the most popular demands of the progressive movement is Medicare for All. To win Medicare for All as well as protect existing programs whose budgets are on the Right’s chopping block, there is a groundswell of energy going into electing its advocates to Congress. The drive to gain and protect social welfare programs (or to have a pro-union National Labor Relations Board, an Environmental Protection Agency actually concerned about climate change, a Justice Department that enforces civil rights, regulatory agencies that check untrammeled corporate power, etc.) exerts a strong pull toward contending for power within the state as well as building mass protest outside of it. What is the logic of demanding Medicare for All but refusing to fight for advocates of that program who can lead its implementation? We Need Orders of Magnitude More Power All versions of capitalism rest on exploitation. But they vary considerably regarding the conditions of life and levels of democratic rights of the subaltern classes. And what gains can be won within a capitalist system does not depend only on outside-the-state pressure; the capacity to battle inside the state is a major factor as well. Having champions in legislative bodies, from city councils throughs state legislatures to Congress, makes a difference. An even larger difference can be made if progressives or socialists can capture the executive. On the local level, the experience of the Harold Washington mayoralty in Chicago and what Mamdani has been able to deliver in just a few months illustrate this point. A governing power strategy aims to take this process as far as it can go. A particular change high on the agenda is eliminating the many undemocratic features of the US electoral system. That means restoring the Voting Rights Act and then going further to abolish the Electoral College , prohibit both racial and partisan gerrymandering, and mandate multimember districts with proportional representation . Winning even some of these requires changes in the political complexion of all three branches of the federal government; that is, as WFP National Director Maurice Mitchell puts it, “to get enough power inside a rigged system to unrig it .” We have a long way to go before achieving that level of “inside” power. Police, Prisons, and the Military-Industrial Complex Even as the functions of the capitalist state have expanded, it remains true that “a standing army and police are the chief instruments of state power.” Dealing with the repressive arms of that state — the police, prisons, prosecutorial bodies, and the military-industrial complex that enforces Washington‘s will abroad — is where insurgent electeds face their biggest challenge. And our problems on this battlefront are not limited to our relative lack of political power. The progressive movement lacks a compelling platform speaking to the working class’s concerns about public and personal safety. There is all-but-universal agreement on the Left that the US justice system is permeated by racism, human rights abuses, and an obscene level of incarceration. But that understanding does not automatically translate into a set of policies concerning law, law enforcement, crime, and prisons that actually benefit, and can gain the durable support of, the multiracial US working class along the way. Formulating, implementing, and building support for such policies is both important in itself and indispensable for eroding the current strength of police unions, “law-and-order” demagogues, and the racist right in general. (The same we-must-learn-more approach applies to numerous other policy areas.) The US left is at an early stage of learning how to navigate these challenges. But there is experience to draw upon for lessons, from that of the Harold Washington and Zohran Mamdani administrations and from the still-young national effort to elect district attorneys who advocate deepgoing reforms (such as Larry Krasner in Philadelphia). Another source of lessons is the experience of black communities after passage of the 1965 Voting Rights Act, which led to the first election of a black sheriff in the South since Reconstruction and a substantial drop in racially biased arrests nationwide. And there are radicals exploring new frameworks for a public safety platform such as “law of the weakest” and “ carceral minimalism .” Further, anti-capitalists who have captured substantial governing power at the local or state level will almost certainly face situations where the government they lead takes repressive measures against the social forces that they represent. But this road must be traveled because two other things are simultaneously true: One, it is more possible to erode the power of these bodies if a radical movement has champions within the state as well as outside of it; and two, every step to weaken the repressive apparatus contributes to harm reduction and to increasing the space available for insurgent movements to organize for power. Empire and the Military-Industrial Complex Dealing with the military-industrial complex and the related components of the capitalist state that enforce Washington’s goals abroad is similarly complex. But the extent of policy differences even between administrations that are not progressive shows how much room exists for an internationalist force with strength on both the inside and outside to make a difference in the conditions faced by peoples around the world. Cases in point: the difference between a period when the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action nuclear weapons deal negotiated during the Obama administration was in force vs. one where Trump has torn up the deal, or between an administration expanding use of fossil fuels vs. one making even inadequate efforts to fight climate change. There will be no easy victories on this battlefront. But every bit of progress we do make can alleviate the main source of economic bullying and threats of violence that currently afflict the nations of the Global South. And the outpouring of bottom-up resistance to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the unprecedented upsurge for Palestinian rights, and the unpopularity of the war against Iran has spurred a wider openness to fresh ideas about the US role in the world than at any time since the immediate aftermath of the Vietnam War. Add the growing sophistication of progressive and socialist electoral engagement, and it is possible to envision an administration that would have enough popular backing to abolish ICE, substantially cut the military budget, and take other initiatives that stem from a very different sense of what constitutes genuine security . Vital for the Fight Against Fascism Pursuing a strategy of fighting both inside and outside the terrain of the state is also vital to stave off the threat of fascism. In the United States today, the main axis of conflict is between a bloc of white Christian nationalists and oligarchs driving toward US-style fascism and a larger but more politically and organizationally fragmented opposition. The central task of the moment is to unite and galvanize the anti-MAGA majority so that it defeats the MAGA bloc and moves the country to terrain more favorable for working-class advance. The elections since 2016, especially the 2024 balloting, demonstrated that it is not possible to do that — or to gain influence for the broad Left within the antifascist front — if we only campaign on opposition to Trump and MAGA. We need to advance a positive vision of what we are for as well as what we are against. It is a governing power strategy that positions the broad Left not only as the most dedicated and combative opponent of MAGA but also as a force offering a positive vision of what a post-MAGA government can deliver. And we cannot limit our “positive platform” to domestic issues while only saying what we oppose in terms of foreign policy. Only a positive vision for a transformed role for the United States in the world will be compelling enough to sustain broad popular support and bind together movements and organizations whose main focus is “domestic” issues with those focused on peace, climate change, and international working-class solidarity. Framing that vision as a Third Reconstruction roots anti-capitalist politics in the particularities of US history, especially the central role of the fight against white supremacy. It also signals that even if we achieve that objective, changing the country will still be a work in progress. As with the First and Second Reconstructions, a new round of gains could be thrown back, or a Third Reconstruction government could be a stepping stone toward the radical rupture needed to overcome capitalism. It is by fighting for consistent democracy and maximum change within the capitalist system (whether we frame it as a Third Reconstruction or not) that the working class and its allies learn that capitalism must be transcended. It is also how the popular majority gains the experience of wielding power and learns how to rule. Fleshing Out the Bare Bones We are living through the most intense phase of the sixty-year backlash against the gains of the 1960s in which the black-led civil rights movement was the driving force. There is an all-too-real danger of that backlash leading to the consolidation of US-style fascism. But in the upsurge of resistance to MAGA and the longings of millions for a different and better world, there are the seeds of a new cycle of progressive advance. Within this positive motion, a political trend committed to galvanizing a front broad and combative enough to defeat MAGA and to shaping a progressive post-MAGA administration is gaining momentum. It has a growing cohort of elected officials (most prominently Bernie, AOC, and Mamdani), radical organizations powering electoral work (WFP, Justice Democrats, and the growing “mass politics” wing of DSA), grassroots organizations rooted in issue-based and sector-based fights (a section of labor, Indivisible, the national community organizing networks, and much more), and a media ecosystem (ranging from The Nation to explicitly socialist publications and lefty podcasts). Its core organizers look to and are learning from the civil resistance of Minneapolis ; the electoral sophistication that led to the recent “ Mamdani sweep ” in New York; the grassroots organizing that produced the Abdul El-Sayed–Donovan McKinney–Will Lawrence trifecta in Michigan and Angie Nixon’s win in Florida; and the internationalist passion of the pro-Palestine upsurge. As in most early-stage radical awakenings, practical experience and experimentation run ahead of theoretical synthesis. Big-picture clarity is also hard to come by because the rapidly expanding cohort of self-identified socialists are faced with a challenge for which we have no successful models to draw from: how to overturn capitalism in a developed capitalist country with an established electoral system. There is much to be learned from others who have grappled with this at other times and places, for example: from Antonio Gramsci’s thinking about hegemony, a historic bloc, and war of position/war of maneuver; from the practical and theoretical attempts by communists to take Georgi Dmitrov’s advice to “search out forms of transition or approach to the proletarian revolution.” For the US experience, see especially the chapter “Notes on the Revolution and the 1930s” in Al Richmond’s memoir , A Long View from the Left ; for a lesson-rich history of the Italian Communist Party, once the most vibrant and deeply rooted CP in Western Europe, see Lucio Magri’s book The Tailor of Ulm . Also valuable is a study of the Swedish Social Democratic Party’s “ Meidner Plan ” experience in trying to dismantle capitalism; likewise a look at the years Salvador Allende governed as Chile’s elected president and their bloody end at the hands of the Chilean military backed by Washington. All these and more offer insights into how to fight effectively for governing power, what to expect if a measure of it is achieved, and how it can serve as a step on the path to socialism. Yet we are still traveling an uncharted path. We have nowhere near the power needed to usher in a period of radical reform, much less overcome capitalism. But after many years of the US left being marginal, we have become a force to be reckoned with in mass politics. Making further headway will require a great deal of experimentation, and a consistent practice of honest evaluation and refinement — and we will need to harness all the tenacity, flexibility, and broad-mindedness we can muster as we go.

articles.title: A Labour Prime Minister Inaugurated Britain’s Neoliberal Era
articles.author: Neil Warner
articles.content: When Britain’s Labour Party met for its annual conference in September 1976, the government headed by its leader, James Callaghan, was confronting a severe economic crisis. This included the combination of high inflation and unemployment (“stagflation”) and a currency crisis that would, by the end of the year, lead the government to arrange a loan from the International Monetary Fund (IMF). IMF assistance came with the requirement of steep budget cuts. In this context, conference delegates passed ambitious resolutions that condemned cuts and called for nationalization of much of the financial sector as well as extensive controls over the movement of capital, imports, and company investment decisions. James Callaghan refused to consider such measures. In a speech that historians have often seen as a harbinger of neoliberalism, he told the conference that “the cosy world we were told would go on for ever, where full employment would be guaranteed by a stroke of the Chancellor’s pen” was now gone for good: We used to think you could spend your way out of a recession and increase employment by cutting taxes and boosting government spending. I tell you in all candour that that option no longer exists — and insofar as it ever did exist, it only worked on each occasion since the war by injecting a bigger dose of inflation. While it does make sense to see this speech as a major moment in the history of economic policy, there is widespread misunderstanding about the reasons for its significance. Considering the speech on its fiftieth anniversary can help us to better understand the meaning of neoliberalism and its relationship to contemporary politics. Callaghan and Thatcher It is standard to divide Western capitalist policy regimes since 1945 into two eras, with the later 1970s as a hinge period. The first was an era of close government management of national economies, often called the “Keynesian” era. In the most popular practical application of Keynesianism, governments used their fiscal powers to manage aggregate demand and maintain full employment while preventing economies from “overheating.” The second era was the “neoliberal” one, in which such government interventions were viewed with much greater suspicion, and economic policies promoted the continuous expansion of market logics. In most accounts of the transition between the two regimes, a key turning point is the 1979 election defeat of Callaghan’s Labour Party by Margaret Thatcher’s Conservative Party, which then embarked upon a radical neoliberal program. Thatcher’s election was indeed a dramatic and historic moment, and there were very important differences between her approach and that of her Labour predecessors. Most importantly, Callaghan’s policies were based on efforts to secure agreements with trade unions on wage restraint, whereas Thatcher’s agenda set out to crush the unions through mass unemployment and the exercise of state power. The differences between them ensured that the scale of privatization and deindustrialization in the UK during the 1980s would be exceptional when compared to its West European neighbors. However, some neoliberal policies had already begun under the 1974–79 Labour governments. This included the prioritization of inflation control over keeping unemployment as low as possible as well as policies to boost profits at the expense of wages and some forms of financial deregulation. Labour often justified these policies as pragmatic adaptations to the economic crisis and the demands of financial markets. But this did not place it outside the neoliberal mainstream. Indeed, such pragmatic justifications generally served as a more typical pathway for neoliberalism, especially in electoral democracies in the Global North, than the overtly ideological arguments associated with Thatcherism. However, many interpretations of Callaghan’s speech still present neoliberalism as a quite specific ideological project. The speech’s own framing contributes to this, which could be connected to the fact that it was partly drafted by Callaghan’s son-in-law, the Times economics editor Peter Jay, whom he later appointed as British ambassador to Washington. The most famous sections were effectively a summary of “monetarism,” the fashionable economic doctrine for which Jay had become a prominent enthusiast. Monetarists argued that inflation was a symptom of excessive increases to the supply of money in the economy as a result of various factors, including Keynesian fiscal policies. In their view, which Callaghan echoed in the speech, this simply increased inflation and the “natural rate of unemployment” that was needed to control inflation. Monetarism would go on to provide a central economic argument for Thatcherism and neoliberal policies in general. Here, it was already being embraced by a Labour government. Rethinking the Speech However, there is often a tendency to exaggerate the nature of the doctrinal shift that the speech implied. For one thing, it did not announce a new policy direction. The government had begun spending cuts a year earlier and already implicitly prioritized control of inflation over unemployment. The extent to which Callaghan and his government really believed in “monetarism” is also questionable. While they adopted some money supply targets and “rules” that monetarists advocated, they primarily saw agreement with the unions to restrain wages as the main way of reducing inflation. They also returned to some reflationary Keynesian policies, under better economic conditions, a year later. The idea that governments previously thought they could guarantee full employment at the “stroke of the Chancellor’s pen” was also a caricature. There were long-established understandings that both international constraints and domestic inflation would create difficulties for the pursuit of this goal. This was considered to be especially true under conditions of “free collective bargaining” that British trade unions favored. For this reason, Labour had come to power in 1974 having already agreed to a “Social Contract” with the union movement, which was then very powerful. Under the terms of this deal, the unions committed to wage restraint in exchange for government measures such as stricter price controls, higher social spending, and new union rights. Since the beginning of the 1970s at least, the Labour left had also been proclaiming that there was a crisis of Keynesianism. The Labour right had embraced Keynesianism more fully than the party’s left tendency, which saw it as an approach that avoided reckoning with capital’s structural power and crisis tendencies. For the left, the internationalization of capital and the experience of stagflation in the 1970s were reducing the room for Keynesian policies. They saw this as an opportunity to argue for wide-ranging extensions of state control through nationalizations and planning agreements. In other words, Callaghan’s speech articulated a doctrine that he did not really believe in, and one that would never guide his government’s policies. Moreover, he presented this doctrine in the guise of a conversion from another set of beliefs that had never really existed. Even so, this was still an important moment in the development of neoliberalism. Power and Principles Neoliberalism was never a consistent economic doctrine. While the early Thatcher government also adopted monetarism as a convenient set of tools, it soon abandoned those tools after they proved ineffective, while continuing to pursue the more fundamental goals of privatization, deregulation, and undermining organized labor. The economic policies of another quintessential neoliberal government, the Reagan administration, also departed from the monetarist template. Enabled by the international status of the US dollar, the practice of Reaganism involved “cutting taxes and boosting government spending” (on the military, in this case) in a way that Callaghan’s speech had declared passé . The more consistent feature of neoliberalism was its orientation toward capital, particularly the international variety, at the expense of other social constituencies. We can therefore identify the greater significance of the speech not in the specifics of what Callaghan said but rather in why he said it. He intended the speech to win over international financial markets, where monetarist ideas had become popular. According to Labour’s Chancellor Denis Healey, the government had to speak the language of “monetarist mumbo-jumbo” (as he called it) because it needed to secure the confidence of the markets. Callaghan also wanted to make a virtue of challenging the left-wing activists who predominated among conference delegates. The Labour government had already used concern about the outlook of international markets to push for a renegotiation of the Social Contract, with stricter limits on wages. These increasingly severe wage restraints eventually led to a wave of strikes in the “Winter of Discontent” of 1978–79. This forced another reversal of government policies but destroyed Labour’s central claim that it would bring about greater economic stability through good relations with the unions. The speech showed that Callaghan was becoming more responsive toward international financial markets than toward unions or party activists. There was still a fragile balance in the 1974–79 government, which switched between some of the most left-wing government policies of the past quarter-century and early forms of neoliberalism. But it was increasingly pulled in the latter direction as it faced waves of financial speculation. Meanwhile, social movements that had pushed it toward greater radicalism suffered from disunity, and the alternatives they put forward were vague. End of an Era? If we understand neoliberalism in these terms, it can also help us as we consider the relationship between neoliberalism and contemporary politics. In recent years, it has become difficult to tell whether and to what extent we are still in a “neoliberal” era, as we see ever more dramatic forms of state intervention. This has included the resurrection of national industrial policies, the rise of trade barriers, and threats to the political independence of central banks, notably in the United States under Donald Trump. When we compare this cluster of developments to the emphasis of neoliberalism on markets and “rules” that are enforced by technocrats rather than politicians, they clearly mark an important shift. However, the shift is less clear-cut when we consider the power configurations that were the more fundamental markers of the shift to neoliberalism. The “post-neoliberalism” of the Trump administration, for example, appears in this light more as an amplification of the tendencies that defined the shift from “Keynesianism” to neoliberalism, led by a fraction of capital that is particularly resistant to compromise with other social groups. On the other hand, the new British government of Andy Burnham may express a stronger rhetorical rejection of Thatcherism than its New Labour predecessors. But the struggles Britain has faced in achieving economic growth, combined with the heightened vulnerability of its governments to pressure from bond markets, mean that the space for social democratic policies is currently more restricted than it was during the era of Tony Blair and Gordon Brown. At the same time, the sort of countervailing forces that imposed concrete limits on neoliberalism fifty years ago, such as a strong union movement, are still much weaker than in the past. Until the Left can develop the institutional reforms and social movements that would be necessary to challenge neoliberal power configurations, the most important tendencies that Callaghan’s speech signaled back in 1976 will continue to manifest themselves.
